answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
A consequential accounting method for the electricity-sector could improve visibility into the system-level emissions of customer procurement decisions. Unlike attributional approaches, consequential accounting has the potential to highlight how incremental actions affect overall grid emissions. When used appropriately, these methods could complement existing Scope 2 frameworks by helping companies understand broader market impacts while preserving customer procurement flexibility. Importantly, RPS-compliant in-market procurement should continue to qualify under Scope 2 accounting, and voluntary procurement—both in-market and out-of-market—should remain additive, supported by feasibility safeguards and legacy protections for multi-year customer contracts. This is particularly relevant for those with long-term power contracts that were entered into under existing accounting rules.

While we support the creation of a consequential metric, the relationship between attributional and consequential accounting needs to be more clearly defined. Without clear guardrails, consequential metrics could introduce confusion in Scope 2 claims, reduce consistency in reporting, and increase compliance burdens, especially if used to justify mandatory requirements such as hourly matching or strict deliverability constraints. Applying consequential accounting without understanding the interplay with attributional accounting could unintentionally constrain customer choice, limit procurement options, and undermine voluntary market participation rather than encourage it.

Some methodologies have disadvantaged solutions such as renewable natural gas (RNG) and other lower carbon fuel types, despite their ability to deliver measurable, near-term emissions reductions by displacing higher-carbon fuels. For consequential accounting to be credible and effective, it must treat all energy sources fairly and recognize the full system value of diverse decarbonization pathways, including RNG. Overall, while the development of consequential accounting can be a valuable tool for impact assessment, it should remain optional and should not be used to impose more prescriptive procurement requirements within Scope 2 that reduce flexibility, clarity, or participation in clean energy markets.
